title: Boss: Race morning planner
hook: Build a call time adder and a run pace calculator, then join them into one tool.

warmup.explain: ceil always rounds UP to a whole number, so 2.1 becomes 3.

warmup.q: You want to use a function's answer in later maths. What should the function do?
warmup.explain: print only shows the answer. return hands it back so you can add to it or store it.
split cuts the text at every colon and gives a list of the pieces.

why.heading: Today you build two real tools
why.text: Big boss day, no new ideas. You already know everything. Tool 1 takes a call time like `05:30` and adds minutes to it. Tool 2 takes a distance and a time and works out your pace per km. Task 3 joins them into a race morning planner. Your job is to put old pieces together.

why.heading: Why this is how real code is built
why.text: You will make small functions that each do one job and **return** their answer. A function that returns can be tested alone, reused, and combined. The finished program just calls them. If a tool breaks, you know which small piece to open.

why.heading: Times are text, until they are not
why.text: `"05:30"` is text. To add minutes you turn it into a time with `strptime`, add a `timedelta`, then turn it back with `strftime`. Pace is the same trick, using minutes and seconds `%M:%S`. Pace per km is total seconds divided by km: 55 minutes over 10 km is 330 seconds per km, which is `05:30`.

why.heading: Crash proof at the end
why.text: In task 3 real people type things, so you wrap the input part in `try`. A word where a number should be is a `ValueError`. A distance of 0 is a `ZeroDivisionError`. You met both earlier this week, so you know what to do.

watch.intro: A tiny version of tool 1. Tap Run and look at the two lines.
explain: `strptime` reads the text `06:00` as a time.
`timedelta(minutes=mins)` is the length to add, and `+` moves the time forward.
`strftime` turns the new time back into text, and `return` hands that text back.
The second call crosses midnight and still works: `23:15`.
watch.break_it: Now break it: change `"%H:%M"` in the strptime line to `"%H-%M"` and tap Run. The error is a `ValueError` saying the time data `06:00` does not match format `%H-%M`. That means: the pattern must describe the text exactly. Put the colon back.

tasks.starter:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def add_minutes(clock, mins):
    """Add minutes to an HH:MM time and give back HH:MM."""
    start = datetime.strptime(clock, "%H:%M")
    end = start + timedelta(minutes=mins)
    return ???

print(add_minutes("05:30", 90))
print(add_minutes("23:30", 45))
hints: end is a time. You need to turn it back into text in the shape HH:MM.
The tool for turning a time into text is strftime.

tasks.title: Run pace tool
tasks.task:
Pace per km as `MM:SS`. The line that works out `secs` is a placeholder. Replace `0` with total seconds divided by km, rounded: minutes times 60, divided by km, inside `round(...)`. It must show:

`05:30`
`05:36`
hints: Change only the line that says secs = 0.
Seconds per km is minutes times 60, divided by km. Wrap it in round( ).
secs = round(minutes * 60 / km). Check: 55 x 60 is 3300, divided by 10 is 330 seconds, which is 05:30.

tasks.title: Race morning planner
tasks.task:
Both tools are given. Under the comment, ask `Start time? `, then `Km? ` and `Minutes? `. Show `Pace: ` with the pace and ` /km`, then `Back at: ` with the start time plus the run minutes. Wrap it in `try`: a ValueError shows `Try again`, a ZeroDivisionError shows `Km cannot be 0`. Example: 05:30, 10 km, 55 minutes shows:

`Pace: 05:30 /km`
`Back at: 06:25`
hints: Start with try:. Inside it, three input lines, then two print lines that call your tools.
Km and minutes need int( ) around input( ). The start time stays as text. Then two except blocks lined up with try.
print("Pace:", pace(km, minutes), "/km") and print("Back at:", add_minutes(clock, minutes)). Then except ValueError: print("Try again") and except ZeroDivisionError: print("Km cannot be 0").

tests.expect:
Start time? 05:30
Km? 10
Minutes? 55
Pace: 05:30 /km
Back at: 06:25

Start time? 05:30
Km? 0
Minutes? 55
Km cannot be 0

Start time? 05:30
Km? ten
Try again

recap: Small functions that each return one answer are easy to test and combine.
`strptime`, `timedelta` and `strftime` together move a time forward.
Pace per km is total seconds divided by km, shown as MM:SS.
`try` with `except ValueError` and `except ZeroDivisionError` keeps a tool from crashing.

pc.title: Save the tool as a real file and run it
pc.why: A tool you built on your phone is cool. A tool saved as a file on your PC is real: you can open it any day, change it, and run it again. Today you save the boss build as `pace_tool.py` and run it in the terminal with real typing.
steps: Press the Windows key, type `Visual Studio Code`, and press Enter. It should open your folder PYTHON 30 WORK from last time. If the left panel is empty or different, click **File**, then **Open Folder**, choose Documents, then Python 30 Work, then **Select Folder**.
Hover over the words PYTHON 30 WORK in the left panel, click the first small icon (a page with a plus), type `pace_tool.py` and press Enter. A blank file opens in the editor.

Put your finished task 3 program into the file. The easy way: on this lesson page on your PC, select all your code with the mouse, press Ctrl+C, click inside the VS Code editor, and press Ctrl+V. You can also type it again. The file needs both functions and the bottom part.
Press Ctrl+S to save. The white dot on the tab disappears when it is saved.
Open the terminal if it is not showing: click **Terminal** in the top menu, then **New Terminal**. Type `python pace_tool.py` and press Enter. (If `python` is not recognized, use `py pace_tool.py`.)

The terminal asks `Start time? `. Type `05:30` and press Enter. Then it asks `Km? `: type `10` and press Enter. Then `Minutes? `: type `55` and press Enter. You should see `Pace: 05:30 /km` and `Back at: 06:25`.

Test the crash proofing. Press the Up arrow in the terminal, then Enter, to run it again. This time type `ten` for the km. You should see `Try again` and no red error. Run it once more with `0` for km. You should see `Km cannot be 0`.

Make it yours: change the words `Start time?` in the file to `Call time?`, press Ctrl+S, and run it again with the Up arrow and Enter. Whenever the output looks old, check that you saved. Next time you open VS Code, use **File**, then **Open Recent**, to find Python 30 Work.
